articles.title: A Canadian ranch family's two-decade effort to protect native prairie now covers more than 55,000 acres; auditors have verified its first grassland carbon-credit issuance under a national protocol
articles.summary: More than 55,000 acres of native prairie in Cardston County, Alberta, have become the first property to complete carbon credit verification under the
articles.body: More than 55,000 acres of native prairie in Cardston County, Alberta, have become the first property to complete carbon credit verification under the Climate Action Reserve Canada Grassland Protocol. The milestone was announced on November 6, 2026, by environmental auditing company SCS Global Services and non-profit project developer The Climate Trust. It marks the official verification of carbon offset credits earned through the McIntyre Ranch grassland project. The property is owned by McIntyre Ranching Co. Ltd. and managed by the Thrall family. It is also one of the largest remaining areas of continuous, untouched native grassland in North America. The landowners have placed a permanent conservation easement across the property. This legal agreement prevents the land from being turned into cropland, plowed or disturbed in ways that damage the soil. These protections help keep stored carbon in the ground while protecting the area's natural plants and wildlife.Decades of negotiations culminate in conservation dealThe project's registration under the Climate Action Reserve framework follows more than twenty years of discussions involving landowners, conservation groups and financial partners. To put permanent protections in place and qualify for the carbon market, the Thrall family worked with two major conservation organisations, Nature Conservancy Canada and Ducks Unlimited Canada. Together, the groups created what is now the largest agricultural conservation agreement in Canadian history. The agreement ensures that future generations cannot plow or convert the native grassland into farmland. In return for protecting the land, the project can generate carbon offset credits. These credits represent the greenhouse gas emissions that are avoided by keeping the soil intact instead of converting it to regular farmland. The Thrall family spoke about the history and environmental importance of the property. They said protecting its natural condition was important for preserving the landscape and wildlife. “The McIntyre Ranch is one of the most rare and significant grassland ecosystems in North America given its size and largely unchanged condition. Its diverse native plant communities, healthy wildlife populations, and natural processes still mirror historic grassland dynamics,” said the Thralls. “It is an honor for our family to help protect this land.”Third-party auditing confirms carbon integrityTo make sure the carbon credits sold in international markets are valid, SCS Global Services carried out a detailed technical review of the McIntyre Ranch project under the Canadian grassland rules. The audit team was led by lead auditor Carolin Judd, with Saroop Sandhu serving as technical reviewer. They examined past land use records, models showing the risk of farming in the area, and soil management practices. Their review was designed to confirm that the project met all required standards. Heather Rosa, Director of Carbon Offset Verification at SCS Global Services, said checking natural climate projects is important for building trust in the carbon market. "Grassland conservation is one of several underutilized approaches with high potential to deliver climate change mitigation benefits. As the project developer, TCT's thoughtful and close partnership with the landowners involved with the McIntyre project allowed for a smooth and efficient assessment process," said Rosa. "We were delighted to lead the verification of the first project under CAR's Canada Grassland Protocol to ensure the credits are of high integrity. This is a milestone worth celebrating, one that we hope opens the door to scaled investment in grassland protection across North America." The project was measured against a baseline showing how much soil carbon would normally be lost through farming if the ranch were converted into land for annual crops. By legally preventing this change, the project helps protect large amounts of carbon stored deep in the soil through prairie root systems.Expanding nature-based carbon markets across North AmericaThe successful verification of carbon credits from McIntyre Ranch adds to the growing number of nature-based carbon projects managed by The Climate Trust across North America. With the addition of the 55,000-acre Alberta property, the organisation's grassland conservation portfolio now covers more than 250,000 acres of permanently protected grazing land across 15 separate projects. Since it was founded in 1997, the non-profit has also developed more than 30 nature-based carbon projects. These include reforestation, improved forest management and grassland protection initiatives. Travis Croft, Program Manager at The Climate Trust, spoke about the growing threat to native grasslands and their importance in protecting the environment. “Large expanses of in-tact grassland like this are increasingly hard to find in the Great Plains, yet they represent one of our most important – and most at risk - natural carbon sinks. TCT is thrilled to add this project to our grasslands conservation program to support lasting soil carbon storage and biodiversity benefits,” said Croft. As more companies look for verified carbon credits to help meet their climate targets, project developers hope the McIntyre Ranch verification will become a model for other large agricultural landowners in Western Canada and the United States.You use AI every day. articles.title: Guide dog Eddie has won the 16th annual American Humane Hero Dog Award for helping handler Luis Rodriguez navigate daily life; their partnership has also inspired advocacy for people with vision loss
articles.summary: A world you cannot even see is a scary thought: when the familiar becomes unfamiliar.
articles.body: A world you cannot even see is a scary thought: when the familiar becomes unfamiliar. A lot of people with vision disabilities or blindness struggle with the mundane tasks of everyday life that we take for granted: stepping off a pavement, finding a staircase, moving through a crowded station or crossing a busy road. For someone living with vision loss, these everyday journeys can demand planning and concentration. Not to mention, how isolating and fearful it must feel to go through life with one of our senses muted. Losing confidence in your ability to move around independently can make the world feel smaller.But, a guide dog can make it easier. They are trained to navigate obstacles, they offer more than help getting from one place to another. They can restore independence, spontaneity and companionship. One such guide dog, Eddie, has won the 16th annual American Humane Hero Dog Award for helping handler Luis Rodriguez navigate daily life. The 3-year-old Labrador retriever was honored for changing the life of his owner through his work.A new kind of confidenceRodriguez, who lives in Miami, was diagnosed with retinitis pigmentosa when he was 8 years old. The rare inherited eye condition gradually damages light-sensitive cells in the retina, causing progressive vision loss. His sight continued to deteriorate over the years, and he is now legally blind. As daily life became more difficult to navigate, so did the thought of heading out alone.His wife encouraged him to consider getting a guide dog. He was eventually paired with Eddie through Dogs Inc., and the Labrador became his first guide dog. The two have now been working together for around 18 months. Eddie helps him move around safely, avoiding obstacles and finding stairs and elevators. But the real difference is what this support makes possible: the confidence to leave home, make plans and get on with the day without depending on someone else at every turn.There is a lot more to guide work than simply following a dog down the street. Guide dogs are trained to navigate pedestrian routes, avoid obstacles and stop at kerbs and stairs. They also learn something called intelligent disobedience. If a handler gives a command that could put them in danger, the dog is trained to refuse. A guide dog cannot read traffic lights or decide where its handler wants to go; the person chooses the route and decides when it is safe to cross. The two have to learn to communicate and trust each other.That trust can matter enormously. During a trip to Puerto Plata in the Dominican Republic, Eddie and Rodriguez were crossing a busy street when Eddie suddenly planted his paws and refused to move. Seconds later, a car sped past the very spot they would have stepped into. Rodriguez had to trust that his dog was making the right call, and Eddie did not move until it was safe.More than a guide dogPerhaps the most meaningful measure of Eddie's impact is not a dramatic near miss. It is the freedom he has helped return to Rodriguez. He has spoken about taking a spontaneous ride-share trip to Key Largo to go fishing with his brother, something he says would not have been possible before Eddie. A day out like that might sound unremarkable to many of us. But being able to decide to go somewhere and make the journey without fear taking over can mean a great deal when vision loss has made independent travel difficult.And then there is the other side of their relationship, the one that has nothing to do with harnesses, crossings or commands. Eddie may be a working dog when he is out with Rodriguez, but at home he is also an affectionate Labrador. The 70-pound dog enjoys the yard, curling up on the sofa and his nightly grooming ritual. He is still a puppy at heart. The affection they share is what makes this partnership so easy.Eddie has also helped Rodriguez find the confidence to talk about his experience. A naturally introverted person, he began sharing their journey online through his social media channels, “Miami Guy and His Guide Dog”. Their posts have reached thousands, helping explain life with visual impairment and showing how guide dogs support the people they work with. What began as a way for Rodriguez to navigate his own day has become an opportunity to make others feel less alone and encourage people experiencing vision loss to explore the support available to them.Eddie was selected as the overall winner from five finalists in this year's Hero Dog Awards, which recognise dogs across categories including service and guide work, therapy, military service, law enforcement and first response, and emerging hero and shelter dogs. His award celebrates the work guide dogs do, but also shines a light on a relationship built every day, one journey and one decision at a time.For Rodriguez, Eddie's greatest achievement may not be the award. It is it making it possible to say yes to a day out, a walk or a new plan, without first wondering whether he can manage it alone. And for Eddie, that probably means another walk, a little time in the yard and, at the end of the day, spending time with his favourite person.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.body: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Monday held a telephone conversation with Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy, during which the two leaders discussed the ongoing Russia-Ukraine conflict, recent diplomatic developments and ways to strengthen bilateral cooperation.In a post on X, PM Modi described the conversation as productive and said the two leaders reviewed their wide-ranging bilateral cooperation and agreed to further strengthen India-Ukraine ties. He said he thanked Zelenskyy for sharing his perspectives on the conflict, its humanitarian aspects and various efforts to restore peace.PM Modi reiterated India's commitment to contributing in every possible way towards a peaceful resolution of the conflict. According to the Prime Minister's Office (PMO), he also reaffirmed New Delhi's consistent position that the conflict must be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy and conveyed India's readiness to contribute to all efforts aimed at a peaceful resolution.Zelenskyy, meanwhile, said he had briefed PM Modi on the latest diplomatic developments and ongoing preparations for a meeting in Abu Dhabi. He said Ukraine was preparing on every item on the agenda and called on Russia to demonstrate a similar willingness to de-escalate the conflict.The Ukrainian president also said the two leaders discussed India's potential role in establishing food corridors amid disruptions to grain exports through the Black Sea. According to Zelenskyy, PM Modi had said India was ready to mediate in establishing such corridors, an effort Kyiv hopes will continue."It is important that India identify what steps it can take and what dialogue it can pursue with other leaders to help bring the war to an end. Food security could be one such area," Zelenskyy wrote on X.He also highlighted the wider economic and humanitarian consequences of blocked maritime routes, saying disruptions to grain exports were affecting the global economy and hundreds of millions of people around the world.Zelenskyy said the two sides had agreed that their teams would remain in contact on the food-security issue and other bilateral matters.The conversation comes as the Russia-Ukraine war approaches its fifth year, with diplomatic efforts continuing to find a path towards ending the conflict.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: One of James Bulger's killers to remain in prison
articles.summary: Jon Venables told parole staff dealing with his latest review that he was not seeking release.
articles.body:
Child killer Jon Venables will remain behind bars after he told a Parole Board panel that he should stay in prison.

Venables tortured and murdered two-year-old James Bulger in 1993 after he and Robert Thompson, both then aged 10, snatched him from a shopping centre in Bootle, Merseyside.

Venables told parole staff dealing with his latest review, which took place in private, that he was not seeking release.

A summary of the panel's findings said: "At the outset of the hearing, Mr Venables submitted an opening statement to the effect that he accepted the need to undertake further offending work in custody and so was not seeking release."

The panel considered evidence from probation officers based in the prison and in the community, three psychologists and a psychiatrist.

All bar one concluded that he should remain in prison.

Venables and Thompson led the toddler out of the Strand shopping centre while his mother, Denise Fergus, was paying for shopping at a butchers.

After a three-week trial at Preston Crown Court, Venables and Thompson were found guilty of murder.

The names of both boys were released after their trial.

In June 2001, Thompson and Venables were released on life licence and handed new identities.

A court injunction prevented their new identities from ever being revealed.

Venables was recalled to prison in February 2010 after indecent images of children were found on his computer.

He was once again freed in August 2013 - with a second new identity - and then called back in November 2017 for the same offence.

Parole judges considered his case again in September 2020.

In the latest review, a "victim personal statement which clearly conveyed the devastating impact of Mr Venables' crime and the impact of his offending" was heard by the panel.

Panel members found there were concerns about how well Venables would work with probation staff were he to be released and "how open and honest he would be in supervision".

They said there was "a need for further work in custody to address his sexual interests".

The summary went on: "Mr Venables articulated his protracted and extreme remorse for his crime. Professionals assessed this to be genuine and sincere."

Panel members decided that they were "not satisfied that Mr Venables was suitable for release".

articles.title: Meet Indian-origin Anjali Sud, the new CEO of SiriusXM, succeeding Jennifer Witz
articles.summary: Indian-origin media executive Anjali Sud has been appointed the next chief executive officer of SiriusXM, the American audio entertainment company,
articles.body: Indian-origin media executive Anjali Sud has been appointed the next chief executive officer of SiriusXM, the American audio entertainment company, becoming one of the prominent Indian-origin leaders in the US media and technology industry.SiriusXM announced on Monday that Sud, currently the CEO of Fox-owned streaming platform Tubi, will take charge from January 1, 2027. She will succeed Jennifer Witz, who is stepping down after nearly 25 years with the company, including almost six years as its CEO. Witz will remain with SiriusXM in an advisory role until the end of 2027.Sud, who has served as an independent director on SiriusXM's board since March 2025, brings experience in digital media, streaming, technology and advertising-supported businesses. Her appointment comes as the audio entertainment company looks to strengthen its position amid changing consumer listening habits and competition from digital platforms.“I am honored to lead SiriusXM in its next chapter,” Sud said in a statement. “Premium audio experiences will be more important than ever to the future of entertainment, and I believe SiriusXM can evolve to lead that future.”Who is Anjali Sud?Born in Detroit, Michigan, Sud is the daughter of Indian immigrants and grew up in Flint, Michigan. She attended Phillips Academy Andover in Massachusetts before graduating from the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton School with a degree in economics in 2005. She later earned an MBA from Harvard Business School in 2011.Sud began her professional career in finance and media, working at Sagent Advisors, Time Warner and Amazon. She joined Vimeo in 2014, initially taking up a global marketing role before moving into senior leadership positions.In July 2017, she became CEO of Vimeo, taking charge of the video platform as it shifted its focus towards providing software and tools for content creators and businesses rather than competing directly with traditional streaming services.One of her significant achievements at Vimeo was overseeing its transition into an independent publicly traded company in 2021. She led the company until August 2023.How she transformed TubiIn September 2023, Sud joined Tubi as its CEO. The Fox-owned platform offers free, ad-supported movies and television shows, positioning itself as an alternative to subscription-based streaming services.Under her leadership, Tubi expanded its audience to more than 110 million monthly active users, according to SiriusXM's announcement. The company also expanded internationally and surpassed $1 billion in annual revenue.Her experience in managing both advertising-supported and subscription-based entertainment platforms was among the reasons SiriusXM cited for choosing her.What is SiriusXM?SiriusXM operates a portfolio of audio entertainment businesses, including its flagship satellite radio service, Pandora and a large podcast network. The company reaches approximately 255 million monthly listeners across its platforms, according to its announcement.Sud's appointment signals an increased focus on digital media and streaming as the company navigates competition from music and podcast platforms.SiriusXM chairman Greg Maffei said Sud had built successful consumer entertainment platforms and had experience scaling audiences and expanding businesses supported by advertising and subscriptions.Sud will continue serving on SiriusXM's board after becoming CEO. She also sits on the boards of Dolby Laboratories and Change.org.Her appointment adds another Indian-origin executive to the list of leaders heading major American companies, highlighting the growing presence of Indian-origin professionals in the global technology and media industry.You use AI every day. articles.summary: British comedian and actor Russell Brand was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison on Monday after being convicted of raping one woman and
articles.body: British comedian and actor Russell Brand was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison on Monday after being convicted of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others in incidents spanning 2004 to 2009.Sentencing Brand at Southwark Crown Court, Judge Joel Bennathan said the comedian had displayed a "casual and arrogant disregard" for women and described him as a sexual predator who had used his fame and influence to gain access to victims."About 20 years ago, Russell Brand, you were becoming famous," the judge said. "You were clever — and in many people's eyes, funny and charismatic. You had also become a sexual predator."The 51-year-old showed little emotion as the sentence was announced. He was subsequently led away by court officers, briefly mouthing "I love you" to his wife, Laura Brand, as he was taken to the cells, according to BBC reporters covering the hearing.Brand received nine years' imprisonment for the rape conviction. He was also sentenced to nine months for sexually assaulting a woman at a London bar in 2004, 18 months for an assault at the Choice FM studios in 2004 or 2005, and eight months for a separate sexual assault while working on a Channel 4 project in 2009.The three sentences for sexual assault will run concurrently with one another but consecutively to the nine-year rape sentence, bringing his total prison term to 10 years and six months.The judge said Brand had committed sexual offences against multiple women over five years and that making all the sentences concurrent would not adequately reflect the overall gravity of his offending.Judge cites arrogance and abuse of celebrity statusDuring his sentencing remarks, Bennathan said Brand's fame had helped shield his conduct until 2023, when women came forward following a joint investigation by The Times and Channel 4's Dispatches programme.The judge also referred to Brand's conduct during the trial, describing some of his statements as lies. Addressing the sexual assault at the Choice FM studios, he said the incident involved sustained behaviour and added humiliation in front of others.Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones told the court that Brand had abused the power and influence associated with his celebrity status to facilitate access to women."He used it to facilitate an access to women without which the offending could not have taken place. It also fed his own view that he could commit such offences with impunity," she said.Defence lawyer Ian Winter had urged the court to consider Brand's previous good character, charitable work and efforts to help people overcome drug and alcohol addiction. He pointed out that Brand's only previous conviction was for marijuana possession in 1995.The judge said he had taken the mitigating circumstances into account, including a character statement submitted in Brand's support, and reduced the sentence by one year. He also acknowledged that imprisonment would deprive Brand of time with his children, but said this was a consequence of his own actions.Victims describe lasting impact of assaultsThe sentencing hearing also heard statements from the women Brand was convicted of assaulting. One woman, who was sexually assaulted at a birthday party at a London bar in 2004, said the incident had left her in shock and turmoil and made her feel like "damaged goods".She said it had been difficult to watch Brand being celebrated in the media as his career progressed, adding that his public appearances had repeatedly brought back the experience.Another woman, who was raped by Brand at his home in 2009 after meeting him backstage at one of his comedy shows, said she had been left anxious and humiliated and had struggled with eating and sleeping, as well as periods of heavy drinking.In a statement read to the court, she said she had initially feared she would not be believed because of Brand's fame, wealth and influence.A third woman, who was sexually assaulted at the Choice FM studios, said the incident had a lasting impact on her life and that hearing Brand's voice or seeing his image over the years could make her jump.The fourth woman said Brand had demanded a massage while they were working on a Channel 4 advertisement in 2009 and pressed his face into her groin. She said she had reported the incident at the time, but her complaint was brushed aside by senior management.The women came forward following a 2023 investigation by The Times and Channel 4, which featured allegations of sexual abuse and misconduct against Brand.Brand had denied chargesBrand had maintained his innocence throughout the proceedings, insisting that his sexual encounters were consensual. A jury comprising eight men and four women found him guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.He was acquitted of two other rape charges and one count of attempted indecent assault.Following the sentencing, detective superintendent Andy Furphy of the Metropolitan Police described the outcome as a significant milestone in holding Brand accountable.He thanked the women who came forward, saying they had shown "bravery, dignity and resilience" while revisiting traumatic experiences and facing considerable public and media attention.The police officer said the investigation had focused on the women who reported the offences rather than Brand's celebrity status, and urged other survivors of sexual violence to come forward.You use AI every day. articles.title: In Washington, Bob Barker spent 25 years planting 30,000 trees across 71 acres after buying land to putter around in after retiring; his former pasture is now home to endangered frogs and cougars
articles.summary: Discover how Bob Barker transformed a weedy pasture into a thriving forest over 25 years, creating a sanctuary for endangered species in Washington state.
articles.body: Say the name Bob Barker and most people would probably think of a TV game show. This Bob Barker is a different man whose retirement hobby grew into a forest. KING 5 reported in 2022 that he planted about 30,000 trees over 25 years on 71 acres in Washington state, and he did much of the digging himself. The land had once been a pasture. Today, the report says endangered Oregon spotted frogs, bobcats, and families of cougars have been seen there. It shows what one person's slow, steady work can do to a patch of countryside.A retirement plan that started small Barker did not set out to make headlines. According to the Bellingham Herald, after retiring in 1995, he and his wife, Kazuko, moved to Washington and started looking for a piece of land to “putter around in” and plant trees. He ended up choosing land near the South Fork of the Nooksack River. The land had been logged some time ago and became a wet pasture covered in weeds, blackberries and reed canary grass. Barker was not a lifelong forester. He once worked at a logging camp when he was young, but he spent most of his career in biochemistry. It took him 25 years of steady work to turn that weedy field into a forest.Voles, beavers and plenty of patience The first attempt didn't go well. A hired crew planted the first trees, but voles and rabbits nibbled off and killed most of them. Barker tried again with fresh tricks. He deterred rodents with blue plastic tubes wrapped around young trees, built fences to keep beavers from chewing on them and planted them on raised mounds of soil because of the high water table. KING 5 said Barker figured he could plant about 50 trees an hour with his spade. He also signed up for the conservation reserve enhancement programme, a government-funded programme that pays for planting native trees and shrubs along creeks and ditches.Why a rare frog turned upThe Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife’s Draft Washington State Oregon Spotted Frog Recovery Plan, written by Lisa Hallock in 2013, says the frog was classified as endangered in Washington in 1997. It further states that the frog breeds in shallow waters up to 30 centimetres deep, with short plants and full sunlight. At that time, there were only six Washington river drainages where the frogs survived. In the US Fish and Wildlife Service's final rule, the frog is listed as threatened under federal law effective 29 September 2014. The rule lists restoration planting, together with reed canary grass, among the factors that could affect water temperature and vegetation structure for the frog. So trees alone don't explain the frogs. Barker’s restoration helped recreate some of this habitat, and active beavers helped by opening up parts of the forest.A living legacy for the family The Herald reported Barker’s work earned him the Washington tree farm program’s 2022 tree farmer of the year award. Most of the routine care is now handled by his daughters and sons-in-law. Strict rules on logging by streams mean much of the land can no longer be cut for timber. His son-in-law, Dave Tempero, summed it up: “They were all planted by Bob.” The wildlife news is a bonus, not a guarantee, as planting trees does not help every species. Still, a retirement project built one seedling at a time turned a worn-out pasture into a home for wildlife, including a rare frog.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: ‘There is only the United States of America’: Erika Kirk slams Abdul El-Sayed’s ‘Arab America’ remark after historic Senate win
articles.summary: Erika Kirk, the widow of conservative activist Charlie Kirk and CEO of Turning Point USA, has criticized newly elected Michigan Senator Abdul El-Sayed
articles.body: Erika Kirk, the widow of conservative activist Charlie Kirk and CEO of Turning Point USA, has criticized newly elected Michigan Senator Abdul El-Sayed after he described Michigan as the “capital of Arab America”, triggering a debate over immigrant identity, cultural representation and American nationalism.“There is no ‘Arab America.’ There is only the United States of America,” Erika wrote in a post on X on November 8, responding to a video of El-Sayed's remarks at an Arab American leadership summit.The exchange came just days after El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan's November 3 Senate election, making history as the first Muslim elected to the US Senate.What did Abdul El-Sayed say?El-Sayed made the remarks on Friday, November 6, while addressing the CONNECT Arab America Empowerment Summit organized by the Arab America Foundation in Chantilly, Virginia, near Washington DC.Introducing himself by his full name, Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, he said he was honoured to be the next US senator from Michigan.“I know we're here in DC, which of course is the capital of the United States of America, but Michigan is the capital of Arab America,” he told the gathering.His remarks were part of a broader message about Arab American identity and belonging. El-Sayed argued that Arab Americans were united by their shared identity and, more importantly, by America itself.“What unites us as Arab Americans is America,” he said, adding that some people had suggested there should be an “asterisk” on their American identity because of their parents' countries of origin or the language they grew up speaking.He said he hoped his election had demonstrated that America was big enough to include them.Why Michigan?Michigan, particularly the Detroit metropolitan area, has one of the country's most prominent Arab American communities. Dearborn, a Detroit suburb, is widely recognized as a major centre of Arab American life and culture.The community includes people with roots in several countries across the Middle East and North Africa, including Lebanon, Yemen, Iraq and Egypt. Arab American identity is not synonymous with Islam, as the community includes Muslims, Christians and people of other faiths.El-Sayed himself is an Egyptian-American. The 42-year-old former Detroit health director and public health expert has spoken about his heritage and Muslim identity throughout his political career.His victory over Rogers was particularly significant because his campaign faced repeated attacks over his religion and alleged associations with extremist groups. He denied the allegations, and Reuters reported that no evidence had emerged linking him to the Muslim Brotherhood.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A North Carolina divorce involved three Bitcoin valued at $180,000 and Pokemon cards worth $1,800; an appeals court upheld the crypto valuation and property division but overturned orders for legal and accountant fees
articles.summary: A divorce case in North Carolina involving three Bitcoin worth $180,000 and Pokemon cards valued at $1,800 has resulted in a mixed ruling by the state's
articles.body: A divorce case in North Carolina involving three Bitcoin worth $180,000 and Pokemon cards valued at $1,800 has resulted in a mixed ruling by the state's Court of Appeals. The court upheld the valuation of the couple's cryptocurrency and most decisions on dividing their property. However, it overturned orders requiring the husband to pay his former wife's legal fees and the full bill of a forensic accountant.The case involved Alexandra Warber and Tyler Warber, who married in 2016 and separated in 2022. They have two children and were granted joint physical and legal custody in March 2024. The court had also settled child support and legal fees related to the custody case.The couple went to trial in July 2024 to decide how their marital assets should be divided. The court initially approved an order submitted by Tyler on 23 August 2024. Alexandra later asked the court to reconsider it. The judge set aside the earlier order and approved a revised one on 25 January 2025.Tyler challenged the revised decision before the North Carolina Court of Appeals. In its ruling filed on 4 November 2026, the appeals court upheld most of the decisions but sent the orders on legal and accountant fees back for reconsideration.Judge had signed wrong property orderTyler argued that the trial court should not have changed its earlier decision. He said Alexandra should have challenged the original order before the appeals court instead of asking the same trial court to reconsider it.However, the appeals court noted that the judge had explained what went wrong during a hearing on 2 December 2024.The judge told both sides that the earlier order had not been prepared by the court. He said he might have mistakenly clicked on and signed the order submitted by Tyler.The appeals court accepted that the judge had made a mistake and that there were sufficient reasons to correct it. It rejected Tyler's challenge to the revised order.Three Bitcoin valued at $180,000The couple's cryptocurrency holdings were among the main points of disagreement. The trial court valued three Bitcoin at $60,000 each on the date of separation, putting their combined value at $180,000.A forensic accountant also traced other digital assets held by Tyler. These included money in cryptocurrency accounts and 15 digital wallets.The accountant identified digital assets worth $26,076.86 on the date of separation. This included $6 in a Coinbase account, $800.95 in Binance, $3,147.10 in Moonpay and $22,122.81 across 15 wallets.The court also included $5 from a Robinhood account and $24.03 from a Fidelity account. The total value of the cryptocurrency and other digital assets considered for division was $206,195.89.Tyler challenged these figures but had not presented his own expert or a competing valuation. He had also not objected to the forensic accountant's qualifications or the admission of the accountant's report during the trial.The appeals court found no clear legal error in the valuation and upheld the trial court's decision.Pokemon cards worth $1,800The couple's Pokemon trading card collection also became part of the property dispute.According to the trial court's findings, Tyler had taken most of the collection, including its most valuable cards, from their marital home. Alexandra estimated that the cards left with her were worth $300. She put the value of the cards taken by Tyler at between $1,000 and $3,000.The trial court accepted her estimate and valued the entire collection at $1,800. It assigned $1,500 to the cards with Tyler and $300 to those remaining with Alexandra.Tyler argued that Alexandra had only guessed the value. However, he had not presented any evidence of his own to establish how much the cards were worth.The appeals court noted that a person who jointly owns property can give evidence about its value. It found that Alexandra's testimony was sufficient to support the trial court's decision and rejected Tyler's challenge.Court rejects dispute over car loan and retirement savingsThe appeal also involved a 2019 Jeep Compass. Tyler claimed that $32,485 was still owed on the vehicle when the couple separated.However, he did not provide documents showing who had given the loan, the payment details or the interest rate. He also said he believed that approximately $20,000 was still outstanding.The trial court did not find his claim reliable. It also found that he had failed to show that the alleged loan had been taken for the joint benefit of both spouses.The court therefore excluded the claimed debt from the property division. The appeals court upheld this decision.Tyler also challenged the valuation of Alexandra's TIAA retirement account. The trial court had placed the marital portion of the account at $47,748.22.However, Tyler himself had given the same valuation during the trial. The appeals court said he could not challenge a figure he had previously supported. It rejected his argument.Court upholds unequal property divisionTyler also objected to Alexandra receiving a larger share of their marital property. North Carolina law generally favours an equal division of marital assets. However, courts can order a different division if they find that an equal split would not be fair.The law requires courts to consider 12 factors before making such a decision. In this case, the trial court examined all 12 and found that seven supported giving Alexandra a larger share.It also assigned values to the assets being divided. The appeals court found that the trial court had considered the relevant factors and gave no reason to interfere with its decision. It therefore upheld the unequal division of the marital estate.Attorney's fees and accountant's bill sent backAlthough the appeals court upheld most of the property decisions, it found that the trial court had not properly explained why Tyler should pay Alexandra's legal expenses.The trial court had ordered him to pay $15,261.40 in attorney's fees as a penalty for failing to provide documents and cooperate with the required information-sharing process.However, courts in North Carolina generally require each side to pay its own legal expenses unless a law or agreement allows otherwise.The appeals court said that an order requiring one party to pay the other's legal fees must explain why the amount is reasonable. This includes details about the work involved, time spent, skills required, usual charges for similar work and the lawyer's experience.Although Alexandra had submitted an affidavit listing her legal expenses, the trial court's order did not include these details.The appeals court therefore cancelled the $15,261.40 award and sent the issue back to the trial court for fresh consideration.It also cancelled the order requiring Tyler to pay the entire forensic accountant's bill. This issue was also sent back for reconsideration.The appeals court thus upheld the cryptocurrency valuation, the division of the marital assets and the decision to correct the earlier property order. It overturned only the orders on attorney's fees and the forensic accountant's bill.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Ole Miss investigating "deeply troubling" video of racist gestures
articles.summary: The video, posted on social media, shows two girls making monkey sounds and gestures as they pass by a Ring camera on an apartment door.
articles.body:
The University of Mississippi launched an investigation after a video purportedly showing students making racist gestures on another student's doorbell camera was shared on social media.

The video shows two girls making monkey sounds and gestures as they pass by a Ring camera on an apartment door. The person who posted it said her daughter's doorbell camera captured it and that her daughter is a freshman at Ole Miss and has two Black roommates, CBS affiliate WREG reported.

A university spokesperson told CBS News that it condemned the "offensive, hurtful, and unacceptable behaviors" depicted in the video and that the appropriate university offices and processes are actively investigating the incident.

"It's important to note that student conduct cases, records and any potential disciplinary action are protected by the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA)," the statement said. "We are committed to maintaining a safe and welcoming environment for all of our students, faculty, staff, and visitors and will follow our processes to ensure the well-being and safety of our community."

In a subsequent statement to students, faculty and staff, the vice chancellor of student affairs condemned the behavior depicted in the video and said that it "does not reflect our university's values or the kind of community we strive to be every day."

"The behavior depicted in this video is deeply troubling, hurtful, and unacceptable," Shawnboda Mead said in a statement posted on the university's website .

Mead said staff have reached out to the students directly impacted and will continue to support them through the process. She also recognized that situations like this can cause "hurt and concern" among students and assured that the matter is "being taken seriously."

Mead also urged people to be thoughtful about the information being shared online as one student has already been incorrectly identified as being involved in this incident. She said, despite online rumors, no members of the university's sorority community were involved in the incident.

"Every student deserves to feel safe, respected, and valued at the University of Mississippi," Mead said. "Racism and actions that disparage people because of an aspect of their identity have no place in our campus community."

articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Bihar government on Monday stepped up safety preparations for Chhath Puja, directing district administrations to impose a ban on firecrackers near ghats and prohibit private boat operations during the four-day festival from November 13 to 16.The disaster management department asked district magistrates to identify vulnerable riverbanks, barricade unsafe ghats and deploy adequate security personnel and volunteers to manage crowds."Authorities must ensure the availability of trained divers, swimmers, motorboats and life-saving equipment at river ghats to deal with emergencies. Medical teams, ambulances and Quick Medical Response Teams (QMRTs) have also been asked to remain on standby," the statement read.The department has stressed the need for adequate lighting at ghats and approach roads, round-the-clock operation of district control rooms and regular public announcements through loudspeakers. Electrical installations must be inspected before the festival to prevent electrocution.District administrations have also been directed to draw up disaster management and communication plans to prevent panic and stampedes. Coordination meetings with Chhath committees and continuous monitoring of arrangements have been made part of the safety measures.Chhath Puja will begin on November 13 with the 'Nahai Khai' ritual and conclude on November 16.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Poundland unable to buy new stock as fears over collapse grow
articles.summary: The discount chain is continuing to edge towards collapse and is said to be "running on fumes", according to one insider.
articles.body:
Poundland is unable to buy new stock to fill its shelves after being blocked by its owners from accessing cash in its bank accounts.

The discount chain is on the brink of collapse with one insider describing it as "running on fumes". It has until Thursday to secure a rescue deal.

About £50m has been frozen by its American owner Gordon Brothers, the BBC understands, meaning its 600 shops are running out of stock.

Pressure is building on Gordon Brothers, which bought Poundland for £1 last June, after the owner rejected a takeover bid that could have saved the thousands of jobs currently at risk. Gordon Brothers has been approached for comment.

Poundland has filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators, which protects it from its creditors until Thursday.

Access to funds was limited because of a tension between Gordon Brothers' dual role as both creditor and shareholder, a source said, but added they expected a relaxation of funds in the next two days.

Last week, Poundland boss Barry Williams told staff like-for-like sales, which exclude new store openings, were up 11.4% last week, which included Halloween, but said this was £1.5m ahead of budget.

He said the business made a profit of £18.1m in the year to September, which was a "strong recovery" from the previous year where the business made losses of £68m.

The latest annual accounts have yet to be audited.

Burnham 'ready to support' Poundland staff as retailer faces collapse

Poundland staff protest after chain approach administrators

However, Gordon Brothers has painted a different picture of the business, saying the chain remains "challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading".

It said it had provided significant funding to support the company's ability to trade since it acquired the business.

It has also made £18m, from a combination of debt interest payments and other fees and charges.

On Wednesday, executives from Gordon Brothers will appear before the Business Select Committee with MPs probing whether they are genuinely pursuing a solvent rescue of the business, which has 11,000 employees, and whether every realistic step is being taken to protect jobs and stores.

The session is being held in private given commercially sensitive discussions are still under way with bidders.

On Thursday, the 10-day moratorium to protect Poundland from its creditors expires, but if there is a prospect of a solvent deal, the deadline could be extended.

If not, Poundland is set to collapse into administration and could be broken up.

A source familiar with the sales process said London-based Xyra Group was making "significant progress" in its last minute bid to buy Poundland and could now be the front runner.

An extension of Thursday's deadline now seems an increasingly likely scenario. But such a case would be difficult to put forward if Gordon Brothers continues to block funding.

One observer remarked "if Gordon Brothers is going in front of that committee, you don't want to be giving the message we're pulling up the drawbridge".

Even if a deal is agreed to sell the business as a whole, there is no guarantee a new owner would not reduce the number of stores, but suppliers to Poundland would prefer that outcome to hundreds of sites being sold off to other retailers.

There has been interest from the likes of Poundstretcher, Tesco and B&M in picking up stores which could mean continuing employment for many workers.

The central issue is whether a piecemeal sale would protect more jobs than a buyer willing to keep Poundland trading as a national chain.

articles.title: Russell Brand sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison for rape and sexual assault
articles.summary: The disgraced entertainer was sentenced on Monday following a four-week trial at Southwark Crown Court.
articles.body:
Warning - this report contains graphic content.

Russell Brand has been sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison, after being convicted of rape and sexual assault.

In his sentencing remarks, judge Joel Bennathan described Brand as a "sexual predator" and criticised his "staggering arrogance".

The 51-year-old was sentenced to nine years for rape, with an additional 18 months, nine months and eight months for three counts of sexual assault.

The disgraced entertainer was found guilty of the charges involving four women between 2004 and 2009.

Brand did not react in the dock as he was sentenced. Before being taken down to the cells, he mouthed "I love you" to his wife Laura Brand, who was in the court.

The guidelines state offenders jailed for four years or more for some serious violent or sexual offences will be released at the two thirds point. In Brand's case that would be seven years.

Once released, he is likely to spend the rest of his sentence on licence and will have to abide by specific rules such as wearing a tag. His sentence will not be included in the early release scheme. Sex offenders, along with murderers, are exempt from the scheme.

The judge also paid tribute to the bravery of the women who gave evidence during the trial.

Nine years' imprisonment for anally raping a 21-year-old in 2009 at his home in London

Nine months for sexually assaulting a woman whose breasts he grabbed at a bar in London in 2004 during a birthday party

Eighteen months for sexually assaulting a woman at the Choice FM studios in London in 2004 or 2005, when he grabbed her face and kissed her before touching her breasts and bottom

Eight months for sexual assault while working on a Channel 4 project in 2009, when he laid his head into the groin area of a woman working with him without her consent

In further remarks, the judge said Brand's status protected him until 2023, when journalists from the Sunday Times, the Times and Channel 4's Dispatches outlined a series of misconduct allegations, leading to women making complaints to police.

He said Brand harboured a "casual arrogant disregard to any woman's right to say no to you", while his fame meant he believed "you could act when you liked and how you liked".

The judge said the evidence in the case also showed that Brand's entourage during the peak of his celebrity had "indulged your dreadful behaviour".

Before Brand's sentencing, the court heard victim impact statements from the women he had been accused of assaulting.

One of the women, who spoke from behind a screen, said she had been in "shock and turmoil for years".

"I was extremely upset and traumatised," she said. "I didn't have any respect for myself. I was thinking I was damaged goods - scared of giving off signals that could be taken the wrong way."

She added: "I just want to say - a leopard may change its spots but it's still a leopard."

Brand left victim 'anxious and humiliated'

"Russell Brand has managed to move on," a woman, who was sexually assaulted by Brand in 2005, said in a statement read out in court. "This has had a lasting impact on my life. I recognise this now.

"However, over the years, hearing his voice on television or seeing his image has made me jump. I had a strong adverse reaction hearing his voice."

She added: "Russell Brand is a sexual predator who has no remorse... I just hope he is not allowed to hurt any more women."

A statement from the woman Brand was found to have raped was also shared in court.

"I felt anxious, humiliated and overwhelmed," she said. "I struggled to sleep and eat, I struggled to cope with my emotions, I had to take time away from my work," she said.

She continued: "I had to live with my parents, I sought help and support... I am living with trauma, something I carry every day.

"My confidence and self esteem have been badly affected. I no longer trust my instincts."

The woman said one of the worst parts of what happened was her fear that she might have contracted HIV. She also said she was in considerable pain after the assault.

A woman, who was sexually assaulted while working on a Channel 4 project with Brand in 2009, said in a statement that she was "really upset" afterwards.

"I felt I lost my trust in people, I felt my working environment wasn't safe," she said. "I felt powerless in that moment and it had a knock-on effect on my confidence."

The verdicts were delivered on Thursday following a four-week trial at Southwark Crown Court in London.

Brand was found not guilty of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.

He will automatically have to sign the Sex Offences' Register as part of his sentence because of the crimes he committed.

Laura Brand was seated just a few feet away from the former comedian in the glass-walled dock as he was being sentenced.

Earlier, as he arrived in the dock on Monday morning, Brand mouthed to his wife: "It'll be okay, I don't know how, but it will", and he was seen praying and making a cross sign with his hand as the victim statements were read out.

Brand's barrister Ian Winter KC put forward six character references, including one from Georgina Baillie, the granddaughter of the late actor Andrew Sachs.

Baillie was thrust into the spotlight in 2008 when Brand and Jonathan Ross left offensive messages about her on her grandfather's answering machine during a Radio 2 broadcast.

Winter also told the court that the former entertainer's wife Laura Brand, who gave evidence in her husband's defence during the trial, was experiencing "total devastation" at the verdicts.

He said Mr and Mrs Brand were "currently wrestling with how to exactly explain to a child who's just turned 10 what has happened here".

"It brings home the consequences of this conduct to totally innocent people who have been caught up in it," he said.

Sentencing Brand, the judge said: "I am very conscious that your imprisonment will deprive your children of the presence of their father.

"That sad loss to them, however, is caused by your serious offending."

articles.title: A Nantucket waterfront home held by the same family since 1972 has sold for $42.5 million, setting a new island record and generating $850,000 for a local land bank through the property's transfer fee
articles.summary: A historic waterfront estate overlooking Nantucket Harbour has changed hands for $42.5 million, setting a new record for the island's residential property
articles.body: A historic waterfront estate overlooking Nantucket Harbour has changed hands for $42.5 million, setting a new record for the island's residential property market. The sale of the property at 57 Hulbert Avenue surpasses the previous island record of $42 million, paid by Barstool Sports founder Dave Portnoy for his Monomoy property in 2023. According to The Wall Street Journal, ACK News and Nantucket property records, the estate was sold on November 5, 2026, after remaining with the same family for more than five decades. The transaction also generated $850,000 for the Nantucket Islands Land Bank through the island's property transfer fee. Known as Blue Waters, the property is situated in the Brant Point neighbourhood and offers views across Nantucket Harbour. It was designed by architect William Edward Shepherd and built in 1937. The Fife family had owned the estate since 1972, with the recent transaction marking the end of its 54-year ownership.The property was sold by Andrew, Howard and Richard Fife, along with a Fife family trust. According to deed records cited by ACK News, the buyer was Stella Blue Waters LLC. The estate occupies approximately 0.62 acres and includes a 6,393-square-foot residence with eight bedrooms, a private tennis court and a two-car garage. The home has several features that make it stand out among the island's luxury properties. Its waterfront setting provides direct beach and harbour access, while the main living room features a large central fireplace and a vaulted, ribbed ceiling designed to resemble the interior of a ship.A covered porch overlooking the water offers views of the harbour and passing boats. The estate also has a private red clay tennis court, adding to its appeal as a property designed for both recreation and waterfront living. Its location in Brant Point places it close to Nantucket's harbour while offering panoramic views of the surrounding coastline.How the sale generated $850,000 for the Land BankBeyond setting a new property record, the transaction will also contribute to local land conservation. articles.title: In 2009, Matt Damon co-founded Water.org; by October 2026, its partnership with Ripple had reached more than 1 million people with water or sanitation financing in Latin America and cut transaction fees by up to 66%
articles.summary: In 2009, Matt Damon co-founded Water.org with Gary White to tackle the global water crisis through practical, market-driven solutions.
articles.body: In 2009, Matt Damon co-founded Water.org with Gary White to tackle the global water crisis through practical, market-driven solutions. By October 2026, the organisation’s partnership with Ripple had helped reach more than 1 million people with access to safe water or sanitation financing across Latin America, while cutting transaction fees by up to 66 percent, according to a Ripple press release.The collaboration, which began more than a year ago, now uses Ripple’s payments, stablecoin and digital asset custody infrastructure to move funding faster and more cheaply across emerging markets. Ripple has committed $6 million over three years to support Water.org’s WaterCredit model, which helps families access affordable loans for taps, toilets and piped water connections.What Water.org doesWater.org is a global nonprofit that has positively transformed more than 95 million lives through access to safe water and sanitation. It was founded by Gary White and Matt Damon, who have spent more than 30 years developing market-driven solutions to the water crisis.The organisation’s core product is WaterCredit, a microloan model that partners with local financial institutions to provide affordable loans for families to bring water and sanitation infrastructure into their homes. Rather than relying solely on donations, WaterCredit treats water access as something families can finance over time.That approach has proven scalable. Water.org’s work has reached more than 95 million people worldwide, and its partnership with Ripple is now extending that model into new markets with faster, cheaper capital flows.What Ripple brings to the tableRipple is a provider of blockchain solutions across traditional and digital finance, offering payments, custody, prime brokerage and treasury management services. Its stablecoin, RLUSD, is a US dollar-backed digital asset that can be used as a settlement layer for cross-border transactions.The partnership uses three pieces of Ripple’s infrastructure. Ripple Payments enables faster, lower-cost cross-border flows to Water.org’s network of local financial institution partners. RLUSD provides a digital settlement layer for more efficient WaterCredit disbursements. Ripple’s Wallet-as-a-Service technology helps Water.org securely manage digital assets as programs scale into new markets.The result is a system where money moves faster, fees drop and more of every dollar reaches the people who need it. Ripple’s CEO, Brad Garlinghouse, said the partnership shows what crypto and blockchain can do when applied to real-world problems.The numbers behind the partnershipSince the collaboration began, Ripple’s funding and payments infrastructure have helped Water.org reach more than 1 million people with access to safe water or sanitation financing across Latin America. The partnership has moved more than $3.2 million across four markets.Settlement times have dropped from two to three days to same-day in Mexico and Brazil. Payment processing is now available 24 hours a day, seven days a week, rather than being subject to a single daily banking cutoff.Transaction fees have also fallen by up to 66 percent. That means more of every dollar reaches borrowers rather than being absorbed by intermediaries, a shift that matters enormously when the goal is to extend small loans to families living on tight budgets.Ripple’s $6 million commitmentTo sustain and accelerate the work, Ripple has committed $6 million to Water.org over three years. The funding will support solutions like WaterCredit, which provides affordable loans for families to bring taps, toilets and piped water connections home.Water.org has also received a grant of $1.25 million in RLUSD through the Stablecoin Impact Fund. That grant will expand stablecoin-enabled WaterCredit disbursements into Indonesia, the Philippines and Uganda.The commitment reflects Ripple’s broader interest in using its technology for social impact. By pairing its payments infrastructure with Water.org’s lending model, the company is betting that faster money movement can translate into more people gaining access to basic services.Get Blue and the wider movementBeyond its direct support for Water.org, Ripple is also putting capital to work through the WaterEquity Everspring Fund, a perpetual impact vehicle that uses philanthropic capital to unlock commercial investment in water and sanitation lending across emerging markets. As loans are repaid, capital is recycled into new lending, allowing each dollar to support families and communities again and again.Ripple has also joined Get Blue, a movement launched by Water.org that unites brands, creators, artists and consumers behind a single mission of bringing safe water home for millions of families worldwide. Founding partners include Gap, Amazon, Starbucks and Ecolab.As the exclusive digital asset and FinTech partner for Get Blue, Ripple brings the payments and stablecoin infrastructure that powers Water.org’s ability to move money faster and more affordably to local financial institutions disbursing WaterCredit loans. Ripple’s first year of Get Blue funding has helped Water.org reach 400,000 people, with its three-year commitment expected to support 1.2 million people.What comes nextWater.org’s goal is to reach 200 million people with access to safe water or sanitation by 2030. The partnership with Ripple is part of that larger push, using financial infrastructure to scale a model that has already proven itself at scale.Gary White, Water.org’s co-founder and CEO, said the issue is not a lack of money but how that money flows. He argued that when affordable financing reaches families living in poverty, their daily spending on water becomes a tap or a toilet that lasts.The collaboration between Ripple and Water.org shows how blockchain and stablecoin technology can be applied to humanitarian problems, not just financial speculation. With more than 1 million people reached in Latin America and a $6 million commitment to scale the work further, the partnership is now testing whether faster, cheaper payments can help close the global water gap.You use AI every day. articles.title: For over a century, a Kentucky college has protected a forest used for research and wildlife; when a power company sought a 1.5-mile transmission corridor, a judge rejected its bid to seize the land
articles.summary: A long-running dispute over the future of a historic Kentucky forest has ended in a significant victory for Berea College, at least at the trial court
articles.body: A long-running dispute over the future of a historic Kentucky forest has ended in a significant victory for Berea College, at least at the trial court level. On April 2, 2026, Madison Circuit Court Judge Kristin Clouse ruled against East Kentucky Power Cooperative (EKPC), rejecting its attempt to acquire part of the college's forest for a high-voltage electricity transmission project. The ruling was first reported by WKYT and further detailed by public radio station WEKU and local publication The Kentucky Edge. The case centred on the proposed Big Hill transmission line, a project intended to improve electricity supply in southeastern Madison County. EKPC wanted to secure land through eminent domain, a legal process that allows certain authorities and utilities to acquire private property for public use, even when the owner does not agree to sell.The proposed route would have crossed more than 1.5 miles of Berea College Forest, bringing power infrastructure close to prominent natural landmarks, including East Pinnacle and Eagles' Nest, as well as the college's telescope observatory. Berea College Forest covers approximately 9,000 acres across Madison and neighbouring counties. It is more than a protected green space. The college manages the land for forestry education, academic research, wildlife conservation, recreation and watershed protection. Its uninterrupted woodland is also important to the institution's forestry programme, which relies on the forest as an outdoor learning and research environment.The court's decision focused largely on how the utility selected its proposed route. According to the 14-page judgment, EKPC relied on a computer-based planning system known as EPRI-KY, which evaluates potential transmission routes using engineering, geographical and environmental factors. However, the judge found that the company had not adequately examined the specific characteristics and existing uses of the college's property before settling on its preferred route.The ruling also raised concerns about the lack of meaningful consultation with the college and the wider community during the planning process. By the time affected landowners were approached, the utility had already identified its preferred locations and routes. The court found that the company had failed to properly assess whether its decision would cause avoidable and disproportionate damage to the forest.The proposed infrastructure also raised concerns beyond the loss of trees. The route could affect views around the college's Windswept property, interfere with the setting of its dark-sky observatory and create environmental concerns for the surrounding watershed. The Owsley Fork Reservoir watershed is particularly important because it contributes to the public water supply for Berea and parts of neighbouring counties. Importantly, the college's opposition was not based on rejecting the need for improved electricity infrastructure altogether. Its argument centred on the location of the proposed line and whether the utility had adequately considered alternative routes and the consequences for the forest.EKPC, meanwhile, maintained that the project was necessary to improve electricity reliability for thousands of cooperative members in southeastern Madison County. The proposed Big Hill project included an approximately 8.3-mile transmission line and a new substation. The utility argued that the infrastructure would help address growing electricity demand and system constraints in the region.The ruling did not end the dispute. East Kentucky Power Cooperative subsequently announced plans to challenge the decision, and filed an appeal with the Kentucky Court of Appeals in April. WEKU reported the development on April 15, 2026, meaning the legal battle continued beyond the initial judgment.For Berea College, however, the April ruling marked an important moment in its efforts to protect a landscape that has served generations of students, researchers and the surrounding community. It also brought attention to a broader question: how infrastructure projects can balance the need for reliable electricity with the responsibility to protect historically and environmentally significant land.You use AI every day. articles.title: 19 runners hospitalized after 'unusual symptoms' at California half-marathon; heat exhaustion might be a reason as Santa Barbara temperatures reached 86 degreeFahrenheit
articles.summary: At least 19 runners were hospitalized after experiencing unusual symptoms following the Santa Barbara Half Marathon in California, prompting a police
articles.body: At least 19 runners were hospitalized after experiencing unusual symptoms following the Santa Barbara Half Marathon in California, prompting a police investigation into what caused the participants to fall ill.The race took place on Sunday, November 8, with around 7,500 people participating in the 13.1-mile event. Several runners were taken to hospitals in Santa Barbara and nearby Goleta after reporting similar symptoms whose cause has not yet been established.Cottage Health, which operates the hospitals that treated the participants, confirmed that 19 runners arrived at its emergency departments following the race."We have a larger than expected number of emergency visits that are tracked to participants in this morning's organized run in [Santa Barbara]," the hospital system said in a statement. "This morning 19 participants arrived at Cottage EDs, a number of them with similar symptoms of undetermined cause."The hospital said it was investigating whether the illnesses were linked to the heat or other factors.Santa Barbara police are also investigating the incident. Authorities said they received a report from the hospital about multiple race participants seeking medical treatment for unusual symptoms after the event."The cause of the reported symptoms has not been confirmed," police said, adding that participants who felt unwell should seek medical attention.What happened during the half-marathon?According to the Santa Barbara City Fire Department, 12 runners were transported by emergency crews to Santa Barbara Cottage Hospital, while another three were taken to Goleta Valley Cottage Hospital. Four additional participants reached the hospitals on their own.Emergency crews responded to several locations along the course, including State and Cota streets, between 9.40 am and 10.45 am.The race began at 7 am on Cabrillo Boulevard and finished on State Street. The event was organised by Run Local and sponsored by running brand Hoka.Was the heat responsible?Race organisers believe heat exhaustion and physical exertion could explain the hospitalizations.Event director David Monico told the Los Angeles Times that none of the 15 runners taken to the hospital from the race's medical tent had suffered serious injuries. He said the cases he was aware of involved heat exhaustion.Monico also told Noozhawk that organisers had "no reason to believe that it's anything more than just the heat and exhaustion from the half marathon".Temperatures in Santa Barbara reached 86 degrees Fahrenheit (30 degrees Celsius) on Sunday, making conditions warmer than usual for the event.The race featured water and hydration stations approximately every 1.5 to 2.5 miles. Runners were offered water, Voli Hydration's strawberry lemonade drink and energy gels, while snacks were also available at the finish line.Social media rumours prompt questionsThe incident triggered speculation on social media, with some users suggesting that runners may have been drugged or that drinks at the hydration stations could have been tampered with.However, authorities have not confirmed either allegation, and no evidence of deliberate contamination has been made public.Monico said police were conducting their due diligence because of claims circulating online.Santa Barbara Police Lt. Ethan Ragsdale said investigators had not established a cause as of Sunday evening. He added that there was no specific action recommended for the general public.Police have asked anyone with information about the incident, including participants who experienced unusual symptoms after the race, to contact Sgt. Andre Miller at 805-897-2330.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Newlywed couple renovating a 1950s Long Island home finds a hidden collection of forgotten belongings, including an American flag, a vintage lacrosse stick, and bow and arrow
articles.summary: A newlywed couple found a collection of forgotten belongings while renovating their 1950s home on Long Island, New York.
articles.body: A newlywed couple found a collection of forgotten belongings while renovating their 1950s home on Long Island, New York. Samantha and Ryan DePalma moved into the house in October 2026, hoping to restore its original charm. The discovery came as they examined old doors hanging in the garage and found objects tucked away above them. The items included a tattered American flag, a vintage lacrosse stick, a dusty magazine, and a bow and arrow. An old-fashioned ladder and a hatchet were found later. According to the PEOPLE, the couple was surprised by how well-preserved many of the belongings were, although they do not know how long they had been there or why they were left behind.What did the couple uncover during renovations at their 1950s Long Island homeThe couple’s first surprise came while they were looking for replacement interior doors. They noticed what appeared to be the home’s original doors, which were hanging almost like planks. Samantha and Ryan wanted to find out whether the doors could be salvaged and reused inside the house.Samantha DePalma said, “When we decided to take them down to check their quality and condition, we discovered all these treasures tucked away above them.” The discovery was unexpected because the couple had been focused on the doors themselves, not on what might have been stored out of sight in the garage.The couple uncovered several forgotten belongings in the garageBeneath layers of dirt, the couple found several objects that appeared to have been left in the garage for years. The collection included a tattered American flag with a beautiful eagle atop its flagpole, a vintage lacrosse stick, a dusty magazine, and a bow and arrow.An old-fashioned ladder and a hatchet were discovered later. The couple was surprised that many of the items had remained in such good condition. DePalma said, “We’re holding on to the other discoveries for now, too, because we’d love to find a purpose for as many of them as possible.”“It’s been such a unique experience getting to uncover these little pieces of our home’s past, and we’re excited to see what else we might find!”The couple hopes to turn old discoveries into meaningful home decorationsSamantha and Ryan do not want the discoveries to be forgotten or left to gather dust again. They are considering ways to preserve several items and make them part of their home. The couple would like to have the American flag professionally framed and displayed. They also plan to use its original flagpole for a new flag of their own.Ryan intends to hang the old lacrosse stick in his office. They are keeping the other objects for now while they consider possible uses for them.How are Samantha and Ryan preserving their 1950s home’s original charmThe garage was not the only place where the couple found objects tucked away. While removing old moulding throughout the house, they discovered pennies tucked behind it and decided to keep them. Their renovation has also involved patching walls, painting, dealing with plumbing issues, updating windows and moulding, and restoring the original hardwood floors.They hope to strip and stain the old garage doors and bring them inside, provided the wood is in good enough condition. The couple wants to make the house more functional without losing the details that attracted them to it. Their plans include warm tones, colour, natural textures and thoughtful lighting, while retaining its original character.DePalma said, “We want it to feel like a home that has evolved over the years, with a mix of original charm and updates that make it our own, rather than something that looks brand-new or overly modern.”You use AI every day. articles.title: Lawyers' boycott makes man stay in jail despite bail
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The accused in an abetment of suicide case who got bail from Supreme Court after spending one year in custody had to stay in jail for another
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The accused in an abetment of suicide case who got bail from Supreme Court after spending one year in custody had to stay in jail for another one and a half months as lawyers refused to represent him before the trial court in Baghpat in Uttar Pradesh, which was to pass a formal order to release him and impose terms and conditions for the same.Terming the case "very unusual" and "very disturbing" given that its order had remained unimplemented and the accused was in illegal detention for one and a half months, a bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and Manmohan directed the jail superintendent to release the man immediately on obtaining a personal bond of Rs 10,000 from him.The accused was arrested in Sept last year and granted bail by SC on Sept 28 this year subject to the terms and conditions that the trial court deemed fit and proper to impose. But the court order could not be enforced as advocates refused to represent him in the trial court, probably because the victim in the case was the child of a local lawyer.Alleging the SC's order was being stonewalled by the local bar association by preventing any lawyer from representing him, the accused again knocked on SC's door, seeking its intervention."The deliberate creation of a hostile, terror-filled atmosphere within court precincts to prevent the filing of surety bonds constitutes constructive frustration and subversion of the regular bail order passed by SC. A criminal trial cannot be allowed to continue in a district where the local legal ecosystem, police machinery and local bar have combined to form a singular, hostile front against the accused, thereby creating reasonable apprehension of bias against a fair trial," the petitioner said, pleading transfer of trial in the suicide case out of the state.Besides directing the jail authority to release him, the court sought a response from UP govt on compensation to be paid to the accused for his illegal detention and also directed that the case be brought to the notice of the CJ of Allahabad HC."State is called upon to show cause as to why appropriate compensation should not be awarded to the petitioner for his illegal detention in custody so far, despite the fact that this court ordered release on bail one and a half months back," the bench said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.body: Pune: The city fire brigade recorded 94 fire-related emergency calls between Sunday night and Monday while Pimpri Chinchwad fire brigade received 76 emergency calls on Sunday. This marked the highest number of such calls on Lakshmi puja day since 2021. While no injuries or casualties were reported, officials said most of the fires were caused by firecrackers or diyas. Around 80% of the calls were received between 8pm and 10pm on Sunday.Of the 94, three major fires included one at a plastic godown in Mangalwar Peth. Seven fire tenders were deployed to douse the blaze.The second one was reported after fire broke out at a flex and banner printing unit on Satara Road. Eight fire tenders were rushed to the spot and brought the blaze under control.
