articles.title: Noida Sector 1 sees sharpest pollution spike at 993, but missing data clouds picture
articles.summary: Noida PM2.5 spiked to 993 in Sector 1 on Diwali night; city average peaked at 714.1 before easing. Missing 10.4% hourly data clouds impact.
articles.body: Gurgaon: With crackers still bursting well beyond Supreme Court’s 10pm deadline, pollution levels in Noida saw the sharpest Diwali-night spike among three cities to the east of Delhi, with Sector 1 recording a PM2.5 of 993 micrograms per cubic metre between 1am and 2am on Monday.Noida’s PM2.5 average across reporting stations had peaked earlier at 714.1 µg/m³ between 11pm and midnight, stayed above 650 for another hour and then eased as winds picked up towards dawn. But missing hourly readings at several monitoring stations left gaps in the picture, making it difficult to establish the full extent of the pollution surge.For almost eight hours, the city’s PM2.5 stayed above 300 µg/m³. It took 10 hours to fall below 200, the slowest clearance in five Diwalis. At 403, its Diwali-night average was the third-worst in five years.Ghaziabad’s average across reporting stations peaked at 559 µg/m³ between 11pm and midnight. Wave City recorded 757.8, while New Tehsil-Loni and Ved Vihar-Loni registered 706.3 and 705.6. The city average stayed high at 539.4 in the next hour before falling to 119.6 by 11am-noon.Greater Noida’s average peaked at 296.5 µg/m³ between 11pm and midnight. Knowledge Park-III recorded the highest individual reading at 474, Knowledge Park-V reached 402.3 between 10pm and 11pm. By 11am and noon, the average had fallen to 81.7.But gaps in monitoring left the full picture unclear. Across the 36 hours from midnight on Nov 8 to 11am on Nov 9, 75 of 720 possible hourly observations were missing — 10.4%. Greater Noida had 40 missing readings out of 180 across five stations (22.2%). Gaur Yamuna City reported no data for the entire period; the other four stations had one missing reading at Knowledge Park-III and three at Shiv Nadar University.Noida had 20 missing readings out of 252 across seven stations. Ghaziabad had 15 out of 288 across eight. In Noida, Sector 125 missed five readings, Sector 62 seven, Sector 110 four and Sector 39 four. In Ghaziabad, Sanjay Nagar had 10 missing readings, Loni four and Vasundhara one.Each gap represents a station’s hourly observation, not an entire station being offline.The gaps are crucial because a city’s hourly average uses only stations reporting at that time. When readings are missing, fewer locations contribute to the average data, leaving those areas out of the calculation. The average may not capture the full spread of pollution, making comparisons between cities or hours less reliable. A missing reading alone does not prove pollution was higher or data deliberately withheld. It means there is less evidence to assess the air.PM2.5 refers to particles no larger than 2.5 microns — about one-thirtieth the width of a human hair. They travel deep into the lungs and can enter the bloodstream, leading to asthma, bronchitis, respiratory infections, reduced lung function and cardiovascular disease in the long run.“PM2.5 is a real public health issue, particularly in densely populated areas. Fine particles penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream, affecting several organs,” said Arunesh Kumar, director and head of pulmonology at Paras Health in Gurgaon.Children, older people, pregnant women and those with existing heart or lung conditions are the most vulnerable, he said.Kumar advised people to avoid outdoor activity and strenuous exercise when pollution is high, use a well-fitting N95 mask when necessary and ensure suitable indoor air filtration. “Air pollution is not just a seasonal issue. It is a chronic health concern. articles.title: HC gives Haryana 3 months to ensure schools have mechanisms against LGBTQ+ bullying
articles.summary: Punjab and Haryana HC gives Haryana 3 months to ensure all schools have anti-bullying mechanisms for LGBTQIA+ students; CBSE told to enforce 2015 norms.
articles.body: Gurgaon: Punjab and Haryana high court has given the school education department three months to ensure all schools, irrespective of affiliation, have internal mechanisms to address bullying and harassment, particularly against LGBTQIA+ students.The directions cover complaints involving gender, gender identity and sexual orientation, along with broader student safety and mental health guidelines. Justice Manisha Batra issued the order on Oct 31 while hearing a petition filed by Aarti Malhotra, the mother of a 16-year-old student from a leading Faridabad CBSE school who died by suicide on Feb 24, 2022. The family alleged that the student had faced bullying, harassment and sexual assault by fellow students.The court directed that such complaints be handled promptly and confidentially, and that cases disclosing a cognisable offence be reported to police as required by law. The directions are to be implemented within three months of receiving a certified copy of the judgment.The court also directed Central Board of Secondary Education (CBSE) to issue instructions to its affiliated schools within the territorial jurisdiction of the high Court for strict compliance with its 2015 anti-bullying circular and Supreme Court’s guidelines in the Sukdeb Saha case. CBSE has been asked to call for and scrutinise annual reports submitted by schools and take action under its bylaws in cases of non-compliance. This exercise must also be completed within three months.The court directed the Centre to treat the petition, particularly the suggestions on counsellor-student ratios, training of counsellors to support LGBTQIA+ children and sensitisation through school curriculum, as a representation. The Centre has been asked to consider the suggestions in consultation with National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT) and pass a speaking order within six months of receiving the certified judgment. The decision must be communicated to the petitioner.Emphasising the need to move beyond guidelines that exist only on paper, Justice Batra observed, “Guidelines which remain on paper offer little protection to a child in distress.” The court noted that CBSE’s 2015 anti-bullying circular was already in force when the 16-year-old child faced harassment. It also observed that the school had been informed about his condition by his mother and treating psychologist. The central issue, the court said, was the effective implementation of existing guidelines at the school level.The court referred to SC judgment in the Sukdeb Saha case, which laid down binding guidelines for preventing student suicides and ensuring mental health support in educational institutions across the country. These include appointment of at least one qualified counsellor, psychologist or social worker in institutions with 100 or more students, maintaining optimal student-to-counsellor ratios, and training teaching, non-teaching and administrative staff to deal sensitively with vulnerable and marginalised students, including those from LGBTQ+ communities.SC guidelines also require educational institutions to establish confidential and accessible mechanisms for reporting and addressing sexual assault, harassment, ragging and bullying. HC highlighted that failure to take timely or adequate action, particularly where institutional neglect contributes to a student’s self-harm or suicide, shall be treated as institutional culpability, attracting regulatory and legal consequences.Principal secretary, education department, Vijay Dhaiya said, “The court has directed compliance within three months from receipt of a certified copy of the judgment. The department shall ensure implementation accordingly.”The 16-year-old boy, a Class X student of Delhi Public Schoolat Sector 81 in Greater Faridabad died by suicide on Feb 24, 2022. Malhotra, who worked as an art teacher at the same school, alleged her son had faced sustained bullying, humiliation, and physical and sexual harassment by fellow students from Class VI onwards because his artistic interests and mannerisms were perceived as effeminate. The petition also referred to cyberbullying through fake social media accounts.According to the petition, the child suffered from anxiety, panic attacks, depression and post-traumatic stress disorder. His treating psychologist had advised the school to take adequate action, and his mother had emailed the principal in Sept 2021 naming students allegedly involved in the harassment. However, she alleged the school failed to act effectively.The teenager left behind a handwritten note blaming the school for his death. An FIR was registered the following day under Section 306 of the IPC at BPTP police station in Faridabad.Speaking after the court’s order, Malhotra said her fight was no longer only about seeking justice for her son but also about ensuring that no other child has to endure a similar experience in silence. “What happened to my child should never happen to any other child. I am fighting this battle for all those children who are suffering silently, who are being bullied or harassed but are unable to come forward and speak about what they are going through. My son may not be here to witness this small victory or read about it, but I believe he is watching everything from above. I hope this fight brings some protection and hope to children who are still struggling alone,” she said.Malhotra had initially sought a CBI investigation and monitoring of the probe but later gave up the demand for a CBI inquiry. HC dismissed the monitoring plea as infructuous, noting that police had already filed the final report before the trial court on Dec 6, 2022. It allowed her to raise grievances on alleged deficiencies in the investigation before the competent court. HC clarified that it was not expressing any opinion on the criminal liability of the accused and that the trial court would decide the case independently on the basis of evidence.After the Panchkula classroom assault incident, Haryana govt had proposed several student mental health measures, including SAATH project for structured counselling and early detection of anxiety, depression, bullying and behavioural changes. The initiative will follow a five-stage support and referral mechanism, backed by 122 trained counsellors and around 400 trained teachers across 200 govt schools.
